summary:
## Core Fundamentals

- **Camera Settings**: Turn off **camera shake**. Use **Ball Cam** ~90% of the time, switching to **Car Cam** only when rotating back to grab boost or avoid teammates.
- **Movement**: Prioritize **half-flips** over reversing to maintain momentum. When landing from the air, hold **powerslide** to conserve momentum for a quick recovery.
- **Boost Management**: Learn **boost pad paths** and conserve boost, especially on defense. Wasting boost leaves you unable to clear or counter-attack.
- **Positioning**: Always try to **face the ball** to react quickly. Keep your wheels on the ground when near the play to avoid getting caught mid-flip.

## Mechanics & Training

- **Free Play & Training Packs**: Spend significant time in **Free Play**, as it offers the most time on the ball. If you can't find a training pack for a specific need, **create your own**.
- **Workshop Maps**: PC players should use **workshop maps** (e.g., rings, speed trials) to improve aerial car control.
- **Key Mechanics to Learn**:
  - **Power Shots**: Essential for every aspect of the game. Hit the ball with the corner of your car.
  - **Side Flick**: An easy and effective flick for beginners that allows for fast recovery.
  - **Low 50/50**: A great way to maintain possession by driving under a jumping opponent.
  - **Double Taps**: Helps with reading bounces, spacing, and provides a powerful scoring option.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Create a **focused training routine** that targets your specific weaknesses (e.g., first touches, shooting) rather than just practicing flashy mechanics you'll rarely use in-game.

## Strategy & Game Sense

- **Possession vs. Booming**: Don't just boom the ball away. When you have time and space, **control the ball** to maintain pressure. Boom a clear only when necessary to relieve pressure.
- **50/50s**: If you're under pressure and can't control the ball, **force a 50/50**. It buys time for your team and prevents the opponent from getting a free play.
- **Defensive Clears**: When in doubt, clear the ball into **your own corner**. This is safer than a midfield clear which can set up a shot for the opponent.
- **First Man's Role**: As the **First Man**, your job is to **challenge the ball carrier**. This forces the opponent to act and creates opportunities for your teammates behind you.

> [!TIP]
> While rotating back, look for **disruptive plays** like bumps, demos, or a quick challenge to interrupt the opponent's attack.

## Mindset & Improvement

- **Rank is Not Everything**: Focus on **long-term improvement**, not your current rank. You can be getting better even if your rank temporarily drops.
- **Learn from Replays & Losses**: **Watch your own replays** to identify mistakes without the pressure of playing. View every **loss as a learning opportunity**.
- **Avoid Autopilot and Hesitation**: Play actively and consciously. **Don't hesitate**—make a quick decision and commit to it. It's better to be decisive and wrong than hesitant and late.
- **Be a Good Teammate**: If you're feeling lost, focus on supporting your team. Play safe, give them space, and be the teammate you would want to have.

> [!NOTE]
> This is a video game. Maintaining a **positive mental state** is crucial. You will play worse when tilted, so stay in check for better performance and more enjoyment.
transcription:
## Introduction & Just Getting Started

50 Rocket League tips for beginner to advanced players. Some of these you would have heard of before, but I tried to make it not too much of the standard stuff. Regardless of whether or not you are a beginner or a more advanced player, I recommend you watch all the way through to the end because there is always something new to learn.

Yes, if you are brand new to the game, I'm putting this first: just please play the game. You need to first actually get some hours in so you can start to even understand what you don't understand. Don't worry about fancy mechanics or how to rotate or how to do this and that. Just focus on hitting the ball and keeping the game installed.

## Essential Settings & Camera Control

If you are newer and you want some good settings to start off with, or always want to try out some new ones, I would say that I have pretty stock standard settings that you should try out. For you newer players almost anything is better than default, but these settings are ones that are almost identical to a lot of the pros, so start with these. Oh and also, turn off camera shake.

You have two camera states: ball cam and car cam. Now when you're starting off, I recommend you use ball cam 90% of the time. It's gonna make it easier to track the ball as it makes its way around the field. And even though it may feel a bit off-putting, it's something you do need to get used to.

The only time I recommend turning on car cam when you're starting out is when you're on your way back to defense so you can go over some of the boost pads or to make sure that you don't bump your own teammates.

## Core Movement & Momentum

Your car doesn't matter. You can use anything. Yes, there are cars that people prefer, but you can use anything and it can be viable. Just go with something you like and stick with it.

If you are someone that reverses when out of position, stop. Reversing is only helpful in very, very specific situations. Instead, it is a lot better for you to quickly half flip and start driving in the other direction. This way you maintain momentum and don't end up weirdly stopping and starting.

Very simple tip: boost is one of the most important aspects of this game, and so it's important you know where all the pads are in order to keep stocked up on boost the entire time. To learn this you can just go into free play, turn off the unlimited boost, and work your way around the field making little paths to yourself that you can then use in game.

## Recovery, Free Play, and Awareness

Whenever you're landing badly from a bump or an aerial or just in general, always hold powerslide. It lets your wheels slide which carries your momentum, which you can then use to half flip or side flip to get yourself back into the game.

It might seem boring to you lower ranks, but please trust me, the more you play the more you're going to want to sit in free play. It's the most time you can have on the ball and so it's easily one of the best ways to improve all the different mechanical aspects of your game. Make sure you spend some time in here between your games just to warm up or just to keep yourself warm.

The right stick is used to look around the field and to see what's going on outside of your camera view. Not enough people use it. Even I barely use it, which is something I have been meaning to change for a while now. Get used to using it every now and then to keep tabs on where your teammates and opponents are and so you can better judge your positioning and decision making during the game.

## Smarter Challenges and Fundamental Skills

Lower rank players have this issue quite a bit. They tend to flip into everything. Just don't. A lot of the time you can just take a little touch or just keep your wheels on the ground and drive into the ball. This way you have a fast recovery, you have the chance to bump or demo the opponent behind the ball, you can save your flip to move after the challenge, and you don't end up bouncing out of the 50/50 in a weird way because your flip sent you way off path.

Power shots are essential to every aspect of this game. Not only scoring and shooting, but also clears, saves, passes and just knowing how to get power out of every situation. Making sure you're hitting the ball with the corner of your car in order to generate the most power is needed across every rank, so practice whenever you can.

Watching YouTube videos are great but you don't get the full picture. When you watch someone's stream, you get to see the entire game, not just the highlights. This way you will find it a lot easier to follow someone's thought process during a play and you can have a better time learning from them than if you were just watching people hit clips over and over on YouTube.

## Advanced Recovery and Practice Mindset

Something I have a bad habit of doing is holding down accelerate non-stop. But when I'm landing in those awkward positions where I'm having to power slide and flip out to get back my momentum, if I'm holding accelerate while sliding the wrong way it's gonna make my recovery a little messy. Instead, if you are landing the wrong way, just hold powerslide for that brief moment that you land, and only accelerate once you have started the half flip or the movement out of the awkward landing. That might seem a bit complicated, I hope that does make sense.

Casual matches are a great way to try out new mechanics or a different way of playing if you feel a little worried about your performance in ranked. Oftentimes when I just want to mess around and go for everything, I'll jump into a few casual matches and just ball chase. This helps me focus on my boost management and my recovery time because I'm constantly flying all over the place and trying to get back as fast as I can.

Big advice, something I'm still so bad at. Everyone has that one way they naturally flip towards. For me, I'm comfortable flipping to my left. Make sure you train both ways though. It's going to be so much better for you down the track. This is something you do early on in your game.

Listen to me, your rank means nothing. You can be improving and still be in the same rank, it's fine. You can be improving and still go down a few ranks, it's completely fine. The way you need to look at it, if you're improving but losing, eventually you will have improved to the point you can begin to easily climb back up again. And then eventually you'll improve to the point where you can move past the rank you were first stuck on. Rocket League is a long term game, so stop treating it like you need to be the highest rank tomorrow.

## Starting Dribbling and Game Mentality

The side flick is one of the easiest and most useful flicks for players who are new to dribbling. Once you are dribbling the ball, just simply flip sideways. This not only gives the ball height and speed, it also gets you landing on your wheels a lot faster than any other flick, which is incredibly helpful to give you an easy recovery. There are plenty of tutorials if you need extra help, but this is definitely the flick you should start off with.

This game is hard. It takes thousands of hours to learn the ins and outs and thousands more to learn how to do everything really well. So don't get upset if you're having some trouble learning a mechanic or getting through a rank. Just know that it all takes time for all of us.

## Using 1v1s and Mastering Kickoffs

1v1 matches offer you the most time on the ball and end up being if you make a mistake, you get punished. In game modes with a teammate, you can have backup when you make mistakes. In ones you get scored on, it is a very simple way to see where your faults are and can also be a great way to improve your challenge game, your recoveries, and your shooting.

Kickoffs are one of the things you have to do in every single game of Rocket League and most of the time it happens multiple times a game. So why would you risk not being good at something that you know you have to do every single time you play a match? Learn a really good kickoff and practice it. Understand the ins and outs and train it in a lot of ones matches. For some of you, this might be a very simple diagonal flip kickoff. For you higher ranks, it'll probably be the speedflip. Either way, get one under your belt and start to learn it properly.

## Efficient Play and Learning from Pros

When the ball is in the air while near one of the walls, it can be tempting to just fly up and go for it, but it is much more efficient to use the walls and drive up, then move off the wall to attack the ball. This is going to save you boost, time, and give you more power behind your touches.

This one is huge. The more you watch pro play, the more you start to see how they play the same game as you, just to a different degree. And no, I don't mean that they play Rocket League just like you. I mean when you watch pro gameplay, it's not often all these flashy mechanics and incredible goals. Yes, those still happen, but you'll find that the majority of the game is played through the basics: good touches, good rotations, accurate shooting, and solid passing. These are all things that you can work on bringing to your own gameplay no matter what rank you are and you can get a better idea about all of them just through watching the best of the best.

You do not need to always be flipping. It is important to flip, like when you're away from the ball and trying to build up some speed either moving up the field or rotating back, but flipping all the time is just going to get you caught out of position. In the middle of a flip you cannot really stop yourself or adjust yourself, so you might end up being mid-flip when you have the perfect opportunity to challenge the ball. So if you are near the play or the play is very likely to move your way soon, try to keep your wheels to the ground to give you a faster reaction time.

Possession is key if you want to win. By booming the ball down the field every time it comes to you, you are instantly giving up pressure and giving your opponents possession of the ball. Instead, if you have the time, try to control the ball and dribble or take a touch and then look for a play. There will be times where booming the ball will be a good option, for example where you're being heavily pushed in while defending and you are clearing to give your team time to reset. But if you do have the time to control, take that time to control.

## Advanced Challenges & Defensive Strategy

Just an overall really good pack to practice If you want to better your shooting. I recommend it for people at any rank but obviously it's going to be a lot harder for some of you.

A simple tip that will save you a lot of trouble: right before you're about to aerial through a ball, just make sure you're lined up with it. This way you don't have to worry about air rolling early on to get yourself close to it and you can use your boost instead to get there as fast as you can. Easy.

Like stated earlier, trying to control the ball rather than booming away is really important. But if you're under a lot of pressure and you can't properly control the ball or boom it away, you should try to push towards a 50/50. Moving away from the ball in order to get back on defense quickly or pick up some boost stops you from having any pressure at all. And even if the 50/50 means you'll be stuck with no boost, you are still buying time for your team to back you up. A 50/50 also means that the opponent doesn't get full control over where the ball goes after the challenge, and if you learn how to properly challenge you will end up not only winning but being able to move forward into a play for the team.

On defense, your safety often lies in your own corner. If you have any doubts about where to clear the ball to, it is normally pretty safe to just get a soft touch to the corner so you can then follow up and keep control of it. Try to avoid just hitting it straight down the middle back to your opponents as it's often going to lead to just another shot back at your net. And even if you head it to the corner and your opponent gets possession, you know exactly where they're going to hit the ball and which angle to block, so you have a much easier time defending.

## Training Tools and Positional Awareness

Another very simple tip: if you have the option, then use workshop maps. The basics like rings and speed trials are often good to train your aerial car control. They can both be really good to warm up with before you jump in a ranked and you can find some different kind of workshop maps to work on different aspects of your game.

Another easy tip: face the ball. Keeping your nose of the car facing the ball at all times means you're going to be able to react faster to the play and have an easier time getting involved. If I start turning back too early my opponent might be able to see that and take advantage of the space that I've given them. But if I stay facing the ball, I'm ready to jump in and challenge or move into a defensive position if I need to.

This is something I've started thinking about more recently. Once you know how you need to hit the ball while you're in the air, you should try to think about the best way to position your car afterwards for the landing. If you can get into the habit of making sure you're always landing wheels down on a surface, it will quickly become second nature and you'll have a much faster recovery time.

## Improvement Mindset and Smart Play

Don't worry about losing. If you lose, simply view it as a way to learn from the mistakes in that game and then move on. Letting yourself get upset by a loss and taking nothing away from it is a waste of a game. Always think about what went wrong and where you could have improved or made a difference.

A lot of the time while defending you will see players use up a lot of boost when they don't need to. Wasting boost is bad, but wasting boost on defense is really bad. It's only going to make it harder for you to push out of defense as a team and you'll end up stuck in your net with nothing in the tank. Instead, try to be smart with your positioning and only use your boost when you need to.

If you can't find training packs for the situation you need, just make them. This way you have your own specific trading pack custom built for your wants and needs. No one ever makes their own packs and I really don't understand why.

You only need to win a game by one goal. If there are 10 seconds on the clock and the score is one-nil, it does not matter if regular time ends at two-nil, as long as it doesn't end at 1-1. What I mean is, stop taking those risks just because you want to score another goal. If you want to win games, think it through. Would you rather win or get a chance at scoring that then results in you losing? Just be smart about it.

## Mechanics, Replays, and Team Roles

You hear a lot that mechanics aren't everything and that they aren't really needed at all. Players reach Supersonic Legend with just the basic fundamentals and while that is completely true, it doesn't mean you should neglect them all together. Mechanics make the game easier for you. You'll be able to do things you otherwise couldn't if you hadn't trained them. Not telling you to go out and just be a mech monkey, just something to think about.

Watching your own replays is one of the best ways to improve. You get to sit back without the stress of playing and really just take in all the little mistakes you make as you play. It's not an easy thing to do, looking at your own gameplay and criticizing every single thing about it. But doing so will help you see the flaws and parts of your game that you might have otherwise thought you were doing perfectly, which is going to help you improve later on.

This is something that took me a very, very long time to learn and it is still something I struggle with to this day. Over air rolling is going to make you slow, give you less accurate hits, and it's just an overall bad habit. Instead, you want to only air roll for those minor adjustments in order to be accurate with your touch. By normal aerialing the entire way and then air rolling right at the end, you also allow yourself to adjust to any potential challenges in the air because you're going to be able to angle your car to take a good 50/50.

As the first man on your team, your job is to challenge. Simple. You have two teammates behind you and your opponent has the ball. Why wouldn't you challenge? You are forcing your opponent to do something with the ball. They either have to hit it over you, try to pass it, or accept that they're going to get a 50/50 in which you might win the ball from them. But if it goes over you, then you have a teammate who is in the second man position ready to challenge, and the ball is already moving towards them so they're going to have an easier time reaching it against an oncoming opponent. When first man, try to not play scared and instead challenge and force your opponent to make a play.

## High-Level Tactics and Decision Making

In my eyes, solo queue is better for making you a better all-around player as you're going to have to get used to adapting to different play styles and learning to fit into different teams. But playing with teammates is less frustrating which can be a big thing when it comes to improving, so do what you think is best for you.

While rotating back, there are often times you might see an opportunity that can disrupt the play or catch an opponent off guard, for example a bump or a demo, or even just a slight cut to get a touch while the opponent is trying to control the ball. Instead of just blindly going back to the third man position and not paying attention, try to look for these little moments where you can still remain in the action while also impacting the game around you.

The low 50/50 is one of the best ways to maintain possession and win more challenges. Instead of trying to flick the ball over someone every single time, throw in a low 50/50 every now and then and you can catch them off guard. When they go to jump to defend the flick, you end up sitting behind the ball driving underneath them, where they either hit it straight into you and you still have possession or they go straight over the top and you still have possession. The only way they can win this challenge is to read what you are doing and stay low to the 50, in which case you will have an even challenge. Something you should add to your skill set, especially if you're a 1v1 player.

Hesitation kills confidence. Instead of second guessing yourself and trying to think about what the best thing to do every single time is, go for it or don't go for it, but do not sit there and wonder about which is gonna be better. Just make a decision and stick to it. Yes, it might not end up being the right decision, but it's better to be certain about something than hesitant about everything. Make a decision straight away and stick to it.

## Focused Training and Advanced Offense

Simple advice goes a long way. If you feel lost in the game or you don't know what to do, just be the teammate you wish you had. Play without risks, try to keep a steady amount of boost, and just give your teammates some space. You do not need to be the hero of the game. Just work around your teammates, let them do their thing, and try to be there to help them out.

Autopilot is when you play without thinking, when you just default and you aren't really taking in anything going on around you. Playing this way will mean you aren't learning anything, you're just going through the motions. Instead, try to focus on what aspect of gameplay each game to work on, like boost management or positioning. This way you are staying locked in and will begin to pick up on all the small mistakes happening that you might not first realize.

The one kind of flashy mechanic I tell people they should actually train: double taps are helpful because they help you to learn how to track the ball, read bounces, understand spacing, and also just because they're a really good way to score goals in situations where a simple shot might easily be defended. Definitely something you want to learn and practice as you start to climb in these higher ranks.

Giving yourself a small routine to follow every time you jump on that works on your flaws and the little mistakes you see in your gameplay is an incredibly good way to become a better player in less than a week. Instead of jumping into free play and going for flip resets and air dribbles, focus your time on the aspects of your gameplay you feel you can improve, like shooting and first touches, things that will actually happen in your games. This way you can start to see real progress from your training and not just that one in 100 flip reset you almost hit that one time.

If your opponents are defending well enough and you can't seem to find a way to score, you can always try shooting just to the side of the net. This is often just too far from the reach, but seeing as it looks like it's coming towards net, they jump anyway. It's a pretty simple way to set up a pass to yourself and make some room to give you a better chance of scoring the second time around.

## The Winning Mentality and Conclusion

Having a "I must score" mentality isn't always a great thing. Always play the way that is best for your team rather than for your overall score and points. Hunting for those glory goals and trying to be the player who scored the winning goal can often lead to you over committing to a play and getting your team scored on for your mistake. Just remember you do not have to be the one who scores, because after five minutes the game is over and you'll all have forgotten about it anyway.

This is a video game. You don't need fitness and endurance. It is all about mentality. Keep yourself in a positive mental state. Always remember it's just a game at the end of the day, and also keep in mind that you're more likely to play worse once you are tilted. As long as you keep yourself in check, you'll find your games, your performance, your training, and overall your enjoyment of the game are going to go a whole lot better.

And with that being number 50, that is where today's video ends. But if you do want more tips, feel free to click this video right here. Click the video. Do it, do it, click the video.
